description_full: Hamilton Beach Brands Holding Company, together with its subsidiaries, designs, markets, and distributes small electric household and specialty housewares appliances in the United States and internationally. It offers air fryers, blenders, coffee makers, food processors, indoor electric grills, irons, juicers, mixers, slow cookers, toasters, and toaster ovens. The company also provides commercial products; consumer products under the Hamilton Beach, Proctor Silex, and Weston brands; products under the Hamilton Beach Professional in the premium market; garment care products under the CHI brand; small kitchen appliances under the Lotus brand; home appliances products under the Clorox brand; commercial juicers and sectionizers under the Sunkist brand; and plant-based milk makers under the Numilk brand. In addition, it offers digitally connected devices that enable patients to manage at home chronic conditions that require the use of injectable medications; and other health services, as well as software for home healthcare management. The company sells its products through a network of mass merchandisers, e-commerce retailers, department stores, warehouse clubs, specialty home retailers, distributors, restaurants, fast food chains, bars, hotels, and other retail outlets. Hamilton Beach Brands Holding Company was founded in 1904 and is headquartered in Glen Allen, Virginia.

financial_summary: Hamilton Beach Brands Holding C is a small-cap consumer cyclical business with a $432M market cap on $607M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -2% over the past three years — essentially flat, and a business treading water is rarely a path to compounding.

Returns on capital run at 18% against a 9% cost of capital — a 9-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat, and 23% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $11M in free cash flow — roughly 2 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders. Cash conversion is thin at 0.52×, however, which raises the oldest question in analysis: are these earnings backed by cash?.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.1× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage of 52× is fortress-like.

Shareholder yield of 3.6% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 28% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is.

sect: Its 6% operating margin is roughly in line with the Consumer Cyclical median (8%).
It earns less of the sector's profit than its revenue share would suggest (0.73x).
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-14.1% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 377 companies in the universe; the top four hold 26% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 163% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 20% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 54% and a beta of 0.93, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 1.67 vs 5y 0.87), so read it loosely.
About $2.6M trades a day, enough to build a position, and interest is running hot at 1.7x its yearly average volume.
In past sell-offs it fell 63% in the 2020 crash and 40% in the 2022 bear market.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $27.46 (margin of safety -17%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 38%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $16.98 to $44.65 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
Multiples send mixed signals against Consumer Cyclical peers: cheaper on P/E 7.3 vs 19.3, richer on P/FCF 39.2 vs 16.5 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 105% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 2.6% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 8.1% (vs the 8% bar).
The price implies 14.7% annual cash-flow growth, 3pp more than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 18% clears the cost of capital of 8.8% by 9pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have been steady (CV 0.30).
It runs a 23% gross margin and converts 2% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality is a concern: a weak Piotroski score of 3/9 and cash conversion of only 0.52x.
ROE of 14% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.2x equity multiplier).
It spends 2.2% of revenue on R&D and 0.7% on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 0.1x net debt to EBITDA ($47.3M of cash against $50.0M of debt), with interest covered 52.0x.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 4.1, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at -1.8% over 3 years and 0.1% over 5 years.
At current returns, reinvesting 100% of profits supports about 18.3% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Capex runs only 0.5x depreciation (0.5% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 1, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 73.0% on average.
own: Insiders own 27.9%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 42%.
It returns 3.6% a year to shareholders (2.1% in buybacks and 1.5% in dividends).
people: With about 640 employees, each generates about $948K of revenue, 2.5x the Consumer Cyclical median, and productivity has fallen 2.5% a year.
That works out to $17K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.4M (3x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (2/10, lower is better).
